Dear Administrator Oz:  
  
Borinquen Health Care Center submits these comments as a Federally Qualified Health Center 
(FQHC) that has served the medically underserved communities of Miami-Dade County, Florida 
since 1972. Founded as a grassroots community health initiative in the Wynwood neighborhood, 
Borinquen has grown into a comprehensive primary health care, dental, and behavioral health 
center with multiple locations throughout Miami-Dade County. Borinquen is a Level 3 Patient-
Centered Medical Home (PCMH) â€” the highest designation awarded by NCQA â€” and is 
accredited by the Accreditation Association for Ambulatory Health Care (AAAHC) and CARF 
International. Borinquen provides a full range of services including primary care, pediatrics, 
OB/GYN, behavioral health, dental, HIV services, pharmacy, podiatry, and chiropractic care to a 
culturally diverse, predominantly low-income patient population. Borinquen accepts Medicaid, 
Medicare, most commercial insurance plans, and offers a sliding fee income-based scale for 
uninsured patients, ensuring that no patient is turned away due to inability to pay.  
  
CHCs

underserved 
communities. Borinquen serves a predominantly low-income, culturally diverse patient population 
in Miami-Dade County, including a large proportion of Hispanic and Caribbean patients, many of 
whom are uninsured or rely on Medicaid. Borinquenâ€™s patients frequently face social determinants 
of health including poverty, language barriers, limited transportation, and lack of health insurance, 
making timely access to medications and specialty referrals especially critical. For these patients, 
delays associated with prior authorization (PA) requirements can interrupt treatment, delay 
necessary care, and create significant barriers to maintaining stable health outcomes. These delays 
are common under the current system. A survey from the American Medical Association (AMA) 
found that 94 percent of physicians reported prior authorization delays patient care, while patient 
surveys found the average wait time for a prior authorization decision was approximately three 
days, with nearly one-third of patients waiting longer than one week for a determination.1 At the 
same time, PA requirements continue to impose substantial administrative burden on CHCs 
 
already operating under significant workforce and financial constraints. Borinquen Health 
Center therefore supports many of the changes in this proposed rule because of their potential to 
reduce administrative burden and improve timely patient access to medically necessary care and 
prescription drugs.  
  
Borinquen Health Center appreciates the opportunity to comment on the 2026 Interoperability 
Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule. Our comments are broken 
into seven sections:  
  
I.Interoperability Standards for Application Programming Interfaces (APIs)  
  
Borinquen Health Center appreciates CMSâ€™ continued efforts to modernize interoperability 
infrastructure and improve electronic prior authorization (ePA) processes. We strongly support the 
goal of creating more standardized, interoperable, and real-time data exchange across payers, 
providers, and health IT systems to improve patient access to timely care. For CHCs, 
which frequently coordinate across multiple health plan issuers, hospitals, specialists, pharmacists, 
and behavioral health providers, the current PA environment remains highly fragmented and 
administratively burdensome. These proposals to standardize API functionality and data exchange 
requirements could significantly reduce duplicative documentation requests, improve visibility 
into PA requirements, and streamline care coordination for medically underserved patients. These 
reforms are urgently needed, given the scale of PA activity nationally. Reports show that Medicare 
Advantage (MA) Organizations made nearly 53 million PA determinations in 2024 alone, 
including more than four million full or partial denials.2 Similarly, a Medical Group Management 
Association (MGMA) report that physician practices continue to experience substantial staffing 
and workflow burden associated with manual PA processes, contributing to treatment delays and 
administrative strain across the healthcare system.3  
  
These burdens are particularly significant for CHCs because of the unique patient populations they 
serve and the financial constraints under which they operate. CHCs serve more than 16 million 
Medicaid beneficiaries, over 6 million uninsured individuals, 20.5 million low-income individuals, 
1.1 million agricultural workers, and over 1.5 million homeless individuals.4 Additionally, more 
than 90 percent of CHCâ€™s patients have incomes below 200 percent of the federal poverty level 
(FPL), and many patients experience significant barriers related to transportation, broadband 
access, language services, and specialist availability.5 Delays caused by fragmented PA processes 
can disproportionately affect CHC patients, who cannot afford delays in medication access, 
specialty referrals, diagnostic testing, or behavioral health treatment. For providers operating with 
limited staffing and infrastructure capacity, repeated manual prioritization submissions, varying 
payer requirements, and inconsistent documentation standards divert essential resources away 
from direct patient care and essential services.   
  
Concurrently, Borinquen Health Center urges CMS to recognize that the success of these 
proposals will depend heavily on vendor readiness, operational consistency, and meaningful 
implementation support for safety-net providers. CHCs often lack the financial flexibility or 
internal IT workforce necessary to rapidly adapt to evolving interoperability requirements and 
 
frequently rely on a limited number of EHR vendors and/or third-party technology partners. Like 
many FQHCs, Borinquen Health Care Center operates with a small IT department that supports 
multiple clinic locations and a broad range of health IT systems, including electronic health records 
(EHR), pharmacy management, and patient portal platforms. Our IT team is responsible for 
supporting the full range of clinical and administrative operations across our facilities, leaving 
limited capacity to rapidly absorb new interoperability integration requirements without vendor 
support and implementation guidance. The proposed rule appropriately places obligations for API 
readiness and interoperability on impacted payers. However, absent corresponding readiness 
requirements for vendors, we are concerned that CHCs may face compliance gaps and operational 
disruption despite acting in good faith. CMS should clarify that providers will not be penalized for 
failures attributable to vendors, clearinghouses, or EHR systems outside provider 
control. Borinquen Health Center further recommends that CMS coordinate implementation 
timelines closely with the Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT (ONC) certification 
requirements and establish readiness validation or testing before enforcement begins. Inconsistent 
implementation of APIs and varying rollout schedules across payers could undermine the 
efficiencies CMS seeks to create in this proposed rule.6   
  
CMS should also consider establishing uniform minimum implementation requirements across 
Medicaid Managed Care Organizations (MCOs) and Qualified Health Plan (QHP) issuers, 
including standardized PA data fields, synchronized implementation guide (IG) timelines, and 
clearer operational standards. Without greater alignment across payers, CHCs may face 
fragmented payer-to-payer workflows that increase administrative complexity, create operational 
confusion, and undermine the efficiencies these reforms are intended to accomplish.   
  
Borinquen Health Center is also concerned that the expansion of API-based exchange 
and ePA requirements may significantly increase cybersecurity exposure for CHCs, which are 
operating with a constrained workforce and infrastructure resources. The proposed rule 
contemplates a broad expansion of interoperable exchanges involving sensitive patient 
information, yet many CHCs, particularly those serving rural communities, lack dedicated 
cybersecurity teams or advanced IT infrastructure comparable to those of large health 
systems. While CHCs maintain a dedicated staff, these IT teams are small and usually wear 
multiple hats, meaning CHCs rely on third-party vendors and organizations to assist them in 
maintaining HIPAA compliance and securing their data. Borinquenâ€™s IT team consists of a small 
number of staff members who manage all technology systems across multiple clinic sites, 
including EHR maintenance, network security, and regulatory compliance. These staff members 
manage multiple responsibilities simultaneously, and Borinquen relies heavily on third-party 
vendors and technology partners to assist with cybersecurity protections and HIPAA 
compliance. As interoperability requirements expand, CMS must ensure that CHCs are not 
absorbing unfunded costs associated with cybersecurity compliance, vendor upgrades, API 
integration, or ongoing maintenance requirements. To ensure CHCs can safely operationalize these 
changes without compromising patient access or continuity of care, CMS should provide technical 
assistance implementation guidance, cybersecurity and IT workforce development support, and 
dedicated health IT funding opportunities. CMS should also ensure that the final implementation 
 
framework reflects the operational realities and resource constraints under which CHCs deliver 
care to medically underserved communities.  
  
Ultimately, Borinquen Health Center supports CMSâ€™ broader interoperability goals because 
standardized, timely, and transparent data exchange can improve patient access to care and reduce 
administrative barriers that interfere with essential treatment. However, successful implementation 
will require CMS to pair these requirements with realistic timelines, coordinated national 
standards, robust vendor accountability, and targeted support for safety-net providers. With 
stronger implementation safeguards and implementation support, CMS can ensure these reforms 
improve care coordination and reduce administrative burden while protecting access to care for 
CHC patients.   
  
II.Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs  
  
Borinquen Health Center supports CMSâ€™ proposal to establish ePA requirements for prescription 
drugs. We greatly appreciate the agencyâ€™s effort to extend interoperability reforms to medication 
access workflows. Borinquen Health Center believes these proposals could meaningfully improve 
timely patient access to essential medications while reducing the administrative burden associated 
with manual PA processes. For CHCs, these changes could also improve point-of-prescribing 
visibility into formulary requirements, utilization management criteria, and authorization 
status, helping providers make more informed prescribing decisions during the patient encounter 
and reducing avoidable treatment delays associated with incomplete or inaccurate submissions.   
  
The proposal to require all impacted payers to support ePA for every drug requiring PA is 
particularly important for CHCs. In community health, medication adherence is vital for managing 
chronic diseases, preventing costly hospitalizations, and improving overall quality of life.8 As 
previously mentioned, CHCs serve 3.5 million patients with diabetes, 6.2 million patients with 
hypertension, 10 million overweight or obese patients, and 3.2 million people with depression and 
other mood disorders. Borinquenâ€™s patient population includes a high prevalence of chronic 
conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, and behavioral health disorders, as well as patients 
requiring HIV-related medications including PrEP and antiretroviral therapy. Many of 
Borinquenâ€™s patients rely on continuous, uninterrupted access to prescription medications to 
manage these conditions, and any delays in prior authorization approvals can have serious clinical 
consequences. This patient population is also more likely to experience non-clinical factors of 
health that can make timely medication access critical for avoiding preventable complications and 
maintaining continuity of care. Borinquen Health Center has consistently advocated for 
improved ePA requirements to support operational efficiency and reduce administrative burden 
when 
implemented 
consistently 
and 
supported 
by 
interoperable 
technology 
infrastructure.10 Streamlined ePA workflows would reduce treatment interruptions, improve 
medication adherence, and help CHCs coordinate care more effectively for patients managing 
chronic conditions, behavioral health needs, and other ongoing health concerns.  
  
At the same time, Borinquen Health Center urges CMS to address several operational concerns 
with the proposed prescription drug ePA workflows. Borinquen Health Center recommends that 
 
CMS require payers to expose benefit classification information through the Provider Access APIs 
(via the CRD Coverage Information extension) so providers can determine in real time whether a 
drug falls under the medical benefit or pharmacy benefit pathway. We have concerns that CHCs 
may face a significant burden in managing dual workflows across medical and pharmacy benefit 
pathways. Determining whether a medication falls under the medical benefit or pharmacy benefit 
may not always be clear in real time, particularly for drugs that may be clinic 
administered. Borinquen Health Center also requests clarification on how PA determinations 
would apply in situations where a drug is covered under both medical and pharmacy 
benefits. Specifically, CMS should clarify whether a PA approval issued under one benefit 
pathway would also apply to the alternate payment pathway or whether separate authorization 
determinations would be required. For example, extended-release buprenorphine may be billed 
under the pharmacy benefit when dispensed through a pharmacy but under the medical benefit 
when administered in-clinic by a provider.11 Greater transparency in benefit classification could 
improve prescribing efficiency, reduce inappropriate denials, and support more accurate claims 
processing across payer systems. For example, Borinquen Health Care Center prescribes a range 
of medications that may be subject to dual medical and pharmacy benefit pathways, including 
antiretroviral therapies for HIV management, extended-release injectable buprenorphine for 
substance use disorder treatment, and insulin and other diabetes medications. Clarity on benefit 
pathway classification for these drugs would significantly reduce administrative burden and 
prevent inappropriate denials for Borinquenâ€™s patients.  
  
Borinquen Health Center further requests that CMS carefully evaluate how these requirements will 
interact with pharmacy operations, including 340B contract pharmacy arrangements utilized by 
more than 65 percent of CHCs. As 340B covered entities, CHCs utilize 340B savings to help 
stretch limited resources to provide affordable medications and expanded services for medically 
underserved patients. Implementation of prescription drug ePA requirements will not occur in a 
single system. It will require coordination across entity-owned dispensing operations, contract 
pharmacies, third-party administrators (TPAs), EHR systems, pharmacy management systems 
(PMS), and payer APIs. That coordination can be difficult because PMS and EHR systems may 
not always be fully interoperable or able to exchange complete, structured information in real 
time. Borinquen Health Care Center operates a full-service pharmacy at its main facility located 
at 3601 Federal Highway, Miami, FL 33137, which provides low-cost prescription medications, 
free home delivery, electronic prescription and refill capabilities, and Medication Therapy 
Management (MTM) services. As a 340B covered entity, Borinquen relies on 340B savings to 
extend affordable medication access to its low-income patient population. Coordinating prior 
authorization workflows across Borinquenâ€™s EHR, pharmacy management system, and 340B 
program requires real-time data exchange that is not always reliably available across these 
systems. Pharmacy interoperability stakeholders have identified persistent barriers, including 
limited EHR integration, difficulty incorporating native FHIR content, terminology, and value-set 
misalignment, limitations in medication data standards, and competing vendor priorities.13 Studies 
similarly show that pharmacy access to EHR data can improve clinical interventions, but 
implementation remains dependent on system access, workflow integration, and reliable data 
exchange.14 15   
  
 
These gaps raise concerns for CHCs because pharmacy operations often depend on accurate 
benefit, eligibility, prescribing, dispensing, claims, and 340B accumulation data moving across 
multiple platforms. For example, CHCs may face operational challenges if PA determinations, 
dispensing data, eligibility information, and clinical documentation are housed across separate 
EHR, pharmacy management, contract pharmacy, and third-party administrator systems that do 
not consistently exchange data in real time.16,17 These disconnects can delay medication access, 
create duplicative work, and increase the risk of errors in already complex 340B workflows. As 
we mentioned previously, CHCs frequently lack the financial flexibility and staff capacity to 
absorb the costs of new workflow redesigns without support. Borinquen Health Center urges CMS 
to coordinate with the Office of Pharmacy Affairs (OPA) to provide targeted technical assistance, 
implementation guidance, and funding support to help CHCs operationalize these requirements 
safely and effectively. With stronger implementation alignment and greater transparency 
regarding benefit pathways, ePA for prescription drugs can streamline medication access, reduce 
administrative burden, and protect continuity of care for medically underserved patients.  
  
CMS should also mandate proactive PA expiration notifications to providers via FHIR-based 
alerts. Timely notification of upcoming PA expirations could help CHCs avoid interruptions in 
treatment, delays in medication access, and unnecessary administrative burden associated with 
retroactive reauthorization requests. Evidence shows that proactive outreach before expiration 
achieves positive outcomes in 87% of cases compared to only 25% without such 
notification.18  Proactive expiration alerts could improve continuity of care, reduce avoidable 
treatment disruptions, and support more efficient care coordination workflow for CHCs operating 
with limited staff and resources.   
  
At the same time, Borinquen Health Center urges CMS to recognize that electronic prior 
authorization alone may not reduce overall administrative burden without concurrent prior 
authorization reform. Peer-reviewed evidence demonstrates that providers using ePA submitted 
higher prior authorization volumes, spent more total time on prior authorization activities, had 
greater difficulty identifying step therapy requirements, and experienced slightly decreased 
medication filling rates compared to providers not using ePA.19 This evidence suggests 
that ePA without concurrent PA reform may merely accelerate an inefficient process.  Borinquen 
Health Center therefore urges CMS to pair ePA technology mandates with meaningful PA 
reduction requirements, including extension of gold-carding to prescription drugs and sunset 
provisions for PA categories with consistently high approval rates.  
  
III.Improving Communications and Decision Timeframes for PA  
  
Borinquen Health Center appreciates the agencyâ€™s focus on greater transparency and timeliness 
and 
supports 
CMSâ€™ 
proposals 
to 
improve 
communication 
and 
align 
decision 
timelines for PAs. Standardized decision timeframes across payers and clearer communication 
requirements are critically important for the medically underserved patients CHCs 
serve. Borinquen Health Center is particularly supportive of CMSâ€™ efforts to align PA timelines 
across all payers impacted by this rule by requiring more consistent response timeframes for both 
standard and expedited requests. Specifically, Borinquen Health Center supports the proposed 
 
requirements that PA decisions for covered outpatient drugs be made no later than 24 hours after 
receipt of a request, that standard PA requests for items and services be addressed within 7 days, 
and that expedited requests be addressed within 72 hours. Borinquen Health Center also supports 
CMSâ€™ proposal requiring QHP issuers on the FFEs to provide notice of PA decisions no later than 
72 hours for standard requests and 24 hours for expedited requests for prescription drugs. These 
more uniform and expedited timelines will help reduce unnecessary delays in medication access 
and treatment initiation for patients with urgent or ongoing healthcare needs.  
  
Delays in PA approvals frequently result in delayed treatment, interrupted medication access, and 
avoidable worsening of health conditions. Borinquen Health Care Center has observed firsthand 
how prior authorization delays harm patient outcomes. Patients managing chronic conditions such 
as diabetes, hypertension, and HIV have experienced interruptions in critical medication access 
due to multi-day prior authorization processing times. In some cases, patients requiring behavioral 
health medications or substance use disorder treatment â€” populations that Borinquen actively 
serves through its behavioral health and STOPP-E programs â€” have faced treatment gaps that 
risked relapse or worsening of their conditions while waiting for authorization decisions. For 
CHCs serving medically underserved populations that already face non-clinical factors of health, 
these 
delays 
can 
have 
serious 
consequences. Borinquen 
Health 
Center supports 
aligning PA timelines across programs to improve efficiency and accountability.  
  
Borinquen Health Center supports CMSâ€™ proposal to require payers to provide specific denial 
reasons for all drug PA denials, regardless of submission method. We believe this change will 
allow CHCs to more efficiently correct incomplete submissions, pursue appeals, and resubmit 
requests without the unnecessary back-and-forth that typically delays care. Specifically, requiring 
payers to explain why a request was denied, identify missing or insufficient information, and 
provide actionable information necessary for resubmission or appeal will create a more transparent 
and navigable process for providers operating under significant staffing and operational 
constraints.  
  
Borinquen Health Center also supports CMSâ€™ efforts to improve public reporting of PA denials 
and timeframes. This change is a step towards greater transparency that will improve payer 
accountability and provide policymakers, providers, and patients with better visibility. Borinquen 
Health Center strongly encourages CMS to publish these required PA metrics in a centralized, 
standardized, publicly accessible format on CMSâ€™ website rather than relying solely on individual 
plan websites. Centralized CMS reporting would improve transparency, support oversight efforts, 
and enable stakeholders to more effectively identify trends in delays, denial rates, and utilization 
management practices across payers.   
  
Borinquen Health Center encourages CMS to expand the proposed reporting framework to better 
capture the real-world operational burden that PA requirements place on CHCs and medically 
underserved patients, beyond the appeal and extended review metrics already proposed: These 
additional reporting metrics would be particularly valuable for Borinquen Health Care Center 
because, as an FQHC serving high volumes of Medicaid and uninsured patients, we frequently 
encounter denials and resubmission requirements that consume significant staff time and delay 
 
patient care. Granular data on denial rates by service type and first-pass approval rates would allow 
Borinquen and similar safety-net providers to identify systemic payer patterns and advocate more 
effectively for appropriate utilization management standards.

Breakdown of denial rates by service type or medication category.  
First-pass approval rates prior to any resubmission, extensions, or appeal activity.  
Reporting on denials overturned due to incomplete, inaccurate, or unclear denial

Data completeness and quality metrics.  
  
To further strengthen these reforms, CMS should also consider stronger oversight and enforcement 
mechanisms for plans demonstrating persistent delays, inaccurate reporting, or patterns of 
inappropriate denials. Greater accountability, combined with standardized communication 
requirements and timely decision-making expectations, will help ensure that PA processes support 
patient access to medically necessary treatment. Finally, Borinquen Health Center urges CMS to 
establish automatic approval for PA requests that are not decided within the required 
timeframes. We believe automatic approval upon deadline expiration would be the most effective 
mechanism to ensure compliance and would thus prevent CHCs and patients from bearing the cost 
of payer delays through interrupted care and abandoned treatment.  
  
IV.Reporting Payer API Endpoints and Associated Information for CMS To Publish  
  
Borinquen Health Center supports CMSâ€™ proposal to require impacted payers to report API 
endpoints and associated information for publication on CMSâ€™ website.  Having easy access to 
API endpoints in a centralized location fully operationalizes CMSâ€™ interoperability 
efforts. Currently, a provider must look up each payerâ€™s API endpoints individually to use the Prior 
Authorization API (PA API) to submit a PA request or the Provider Access API to request patient 
data, which can be incredibly burdensome. Having all impacted payersâ€™ API endpoints in one place 
will increase transparency, reduce provider burden, and improve the functionality of the reported 
API endpoints.  
  
For Borinquen Health Care Center, having centralized access to payer API endpoints would be 
especially valuable given the diversity of insurance plans our patients carry, including Medicaid 
managed care organizations, Medicare Advantage plans, and commercial insurers. Our small IT 
team currently must navigate multiple payer websites to locate API information, diverting limited 
technical resources away from higher-priority work such as cybersecurity, telehealth 
infrastructure, and EHR optimization. CHCs often have small IT departments that lack the capacity 
to manually search each payerâ€™s website for API endpoint information. The CHC IT departmentâ€™s 
limited resources could be better spent on strengthening and developing innovative technology 
solutions that benefit patients, such as cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and telehealth. App 
developers and EHR vendors also stand to benefit from centralized, easy access to these endpoints, 
improvements that also directly impact patient care, particularly given that EHR disruptions 
currently occur when hard-coded endpoints become outdated.   
  
 
Borinquen Health Center applauds CMS for the proposed timelines requiring payers to report API 
endpoint information. Existing impacted payers have until 60 days after the effective date of a final 
rule, while new impacted payers have until 60 days before they begin covering patients under the 
applicable CMS program. This approach strikes a reasonable balance between payer accountability 
and operational feasibility. We also support the proposal requiring impacted payers to update the 
information within one week of any changes and verify that the reported information is updated at 
least annually. CHC patients strongly benefit when the CHC and its vendors have this up-to-date 
information, as incorrect information can delay access to and delivery of care. Borinquen Health 
Center commends CMSâ€™ commitment to transparency and encourages the agency to publish API 
endpoint information on its website as machine-readable files. This will help maximize the utility 
and usability of this data. A machine-readable file prevents diverting valuable staff time 
to the interpretation of large amounts of data. As CMS considers the best approach for reporting 
and disseminating this information, we urge the agency to prioritize ease of access for primary 
care providers in safety net settings, especially those in rural areas with limited resources, while 
minimizing duplication and unnecessary complexity.  
  
V.Updates to Patient Access, Provider Directory, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer 
APIs; API Usage Metrics  
  
Information about PA for Drugs in the Patient Access, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs  
Borinquen Health Center supports CMS' proposal requiring impacted payers to make detailed 
information about PA requests and decisions for all drugs available through the Patient Access, 
Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs beginning October 1, 2027. As discussed, PA for drugs 
remains a significant barrier to patients receiving timely care. Having information on APIs helps 
identify opportunities to improve them and monitor overall usage trends for key features. While 
we appreciate payersâ€™ independent efforts to improve transparency around PA, we applaud CMS 
for requiring metrics that will hold payers formally accountable. We encourage CMS to continue 
publishing trends in this data and to seek additional policy levers to ensure PAs are not 
inappropriate barriers to care for patients who need it.  
  
Borinquen Health Center appreciates the proposed timeframe for having PA information available 
through the APIs no later than one business day after the payer receives the request. This change 
aligns timeframes with the current policy for non-drug PAs. We also strongly support the 
requirement that PA information remain accessible for at least one year after the last status update. 
This is particularly critical for the populations CHCs serve. In 2024, CHCs provided care to over 
1.5 million homeless individuals and more than 1.1 million agricultural workersâ€”populations that 
move frequently and may not return to a CHC for months at a time.21 These patients have a limited 
window of engagement, making it difficult to track outstanding PA requests across care episodes. 
Retaining this information for an extended period supports continuity of care and ensures that 
future providers, accessing patient information through the Provider Access API, can quickly 
understand a patient's PA history and better meet their needs.  
  
New Proposed Reporting Levels and Deadlines for API Usage Metrics  
 
Borinquen Health Center supports the proposal requiring Medicaid managed care plans and CHIP 
managed care entities to report Patient Access API usage metrics both by program and by 
plan. This added granularity will give CMS a clearer picture of where access gaps exist and how 
to target improvement efforts. Medicaid patients represent nearly half of CHC patients,22 and 
nearly 78 percent of all Medicaid patients in the U.S. are in a managed care plan.  A significant 
portion of Borinquen Health Care Centerâ€™ patient population is enrolled in Medicaid managed care 
plans, reflecting the broader demographic of the Miami-Dade County communities we serve. 
Disaggregated reporting by program and plan would allow Borinquen and other FQHCs to better 
understand API utilization and access patterns for their Medicaid managed care patients 
specifically. Having disaggregated data helps improve the value of the reported data. 
Additionally, Borinquen Health Center supports CMSâ€™ proposal to align deadlines with reporting 
periods. Better alignment reduces administrative confusion and makes data more meaningful.  
  
Borinquen Health Center also supports expanding the metrics that impacted payers must report for 
the Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer, and PA APIs. Requiring payers to report denial rates, 
timeframes for extensions, and adjudicated appeals for both standard and expedited PAs will 
meaningfully improve transparency and accountability across the system. Beyond the suggested 
metrics, Borinquen Health Center recommends that CMS also require measures of API 
functionality and usability. Although terabytes of health data are transmitted daily, much of it goes 
unused in practice because it is not surfaced directly to users or cannot be incorporated into clinical 
workflows. Borinquen Health Center therefore recommends that CMS track the rate of successful 
API requests, as well as those rejected due to authorization failures or malformed queries, and 
instances where API calls were not received by the requester. Additionally, metrics such as 
structured versus unstructured data in the request response, workflow impact, number of calls per 
query, number of queries per user, and the cost of maintaining each API would help CMS, health 
systems, vendors, and other stakeholders evaluate which APIs deliver meaningful value. With this 
data, CMS would be better positioned to implement targeted policies to address PA issues.  
  
Removing Drug Formulary Information from Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs  
Borinquen Health Center encourages CMS to reconsider its proposal to remove drug formulary 
information from the Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs. While CMS suggests that 
providers already have sufficient access to formulary information through payer websites and 
standard communications, this access is neither reliable nor real-time. As Pharmacy Benefit 
Managers (PBMs) increasingly expand the number of drugs excluded from formularies, formulary 
lists can change rapidly, meaning the information available on a payer's website may not reflect a 
patient's current coverage at the point of care. For CHC providers, who often serve patients covered 
by multiple different payers and lack the administrative infrastructure to conduct manual lookups 
across each, this gap is especially consequential. A provider who cannot quickly determine 
whether a drug is covered, or identify a covered alternative, may delay prescribing or default to a 
less optimal option. Retaining formulary information in the Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer 
APIs would reduce this lookup burden, support better prescribing decisions, and advance the 
transparency goals CMS has articulated throughout this rule. Borinquen Health Center urges CMS 
to weigh this real-world impact on safety-net providers against the administrative burden it cites 
as justification for removal.  
 
  
Federal Matching Funds  
We appreciate the possibility that States operating Medicaid and CHIP programs might be able to 
access federal matching funds to support the new proposals. Borinquen Health Center continues 
to request that CMS ensure safety-net providers are prioritized for these funds, if they are 
available. Safety-net providers, like CHCs, operate on thin margins and would greatly benefit from 
additional funding to help reduce costs such as provider training and implementation expenses. 
Many CHCs are currently under financial strain, with nearly half of CHCs operating with fewer 
than 90 days of cash on hand. The sector's average operating margin has turned negative; one in 
four reporting negative five percent (-5%) operating margins. In response to the unique needs of 
their patients, CHCs invest significant resources into training their staff and patients to meet 
meaningful use and interoperability requirements. CMS should consider the specific investments 
CHCs make, including costs, administrative setup, staff, training,â€‰clinical training, and patient 
education needs, and ensure appropriate interoperability and access. â€‰  
  
VI.Modifications to HIPAA Standards Related to PA  
  
Borinquen Health Center recommends that CMS provide transition support to safety-net 
providers, such as CHCs, during the transition from X12 to FHIR. We appreciate and support 
CMSâ€™ efforts to move away from X12, a legacy system, and towards FHIR standards, an important 
step in enhancing interoperability. However, CHCs and their clearinghouses will need to support 
both standards simultaneously during transition: X12 6020 for claims attachments (CMS-0053-F, 
compliance May 2028) and FHIR/CDex for PA attachments (CMS-0062-P, compliance in 2029). 
This dual-standard burden is real and must be acknowledged. As previously mentioned in this 
letter, CHCs have limited IT staff due to constrained budgets so CMS support would help 
immensely in the transition. Ultimately, Borinquen Health Center requests that CMS 
extend its February 28, 2024, National Standards Group enforcement discretion (FHIR PA API as 
X12 278 substitute) to cover the CMS-0062-P transition period. This would provide relief for 
HIPAA-covered entities to use a FHIR-based PA API in place of the older X12 278 standard 
without facing HIPAA Administrative Simplification enforcement penalties.  
  
Borinquen Health Center supports the use of Clinical Data Exchange (CDex) for PA attachments 
but 
recommends 
specific 
guardrails 
to 
reduce 
provider 
burden 
and 
enhance 
transparency. CDex allows payers to specify exactly what data they need and supports multiple 
formats (C-CDA, PDF, text, FHIR resources). However, CDex also creates a mechanism for 
payers to issue iterative, escalating data requests. Borinquen Health Center recommends CMS:  
â€¢ Require payers to specify all needed documentation in the initial CDex request (no 
drip-feed)  
â€¢ Limit solicited-attachment requests from payers to a maximum of two per PA 
transaction before the payer must issue a decision.   
â€¢ Establish 
maximum 
response 
timeframes 
for 
payers 
after 
receiving CDex attachments.  
  
These actions will set expectations for what the provider needs to share in the initial CDex request 
and limit the burden on CHC providers when providing additional information. This will likely 
lead to more streamlined, expedited ePA decisions, ensuring patient access to crucial health care 
services and prescription drugs.  
Borinquen Health Center supports gold-carding for ePA for prescription drugs. We appreciate that 
CMS has already implemented gold-carding for DMEPOS, for supplies with a 90% approval 
threshold with DME Medicare Administrative Contractors and within the WISeR model,25 which 
began in January 2026 in six states. Gold-carding in ePA will allow certain providers, such as 
CHCs, who have demonstrated compliance with PA requirements to receive exemptions or more 
streamlined reviews. We recommend CMS put out guidance formally recommending payers to 
implement gold card type initiatives and ensure that gold carding privileges extend to all items and 
services for eligible providers, not just specific service categories. This will ensure that providers 
and their patients will experience the full benefits of this strategy to decrease unnecessary PAs.   
Gold carding would help reduce the time staff and providers spend on PA. PA is an expensive 
process for health care organizations that, in many cases, significantly restricts patientsâ€™ ability to 
access needed care. Borinquen Health Care Center staff devote substantial time each week to 
managing prior authorization requests across multiple payers and service lines, including primary 
care referrals, behavioral health services, specialty medications, and diagnostic imaging. These 
administrative demands strain Borinquenâ€™s limited workforce and divert clinical and support staff 
time away from direct patient care, particularly affecting our ability to serve patients with complex 
chronic conditions who require frequent authorizations. It can take weeks to adjudicate the request, 
resulting in costing hundreds of dollars in staff and provider time at a health care organization for 
a single therapy for a single patient. Notably, this effort is not reimbursed and requires valuable 
staff resources. CHC patients often have less comprehensive health insurance plans that require 
more frequent PA than those of higher-income patients. PAs can exacerbate patientsâ€™ health care 
issues and increase the burden of PA costs on CHCs, which already provide lower-cost care with 
fewer resources. Gold-carding would decrease these burdens, and Borinquen Health 
Center supports gold-carding as a strategy to enhance patient access to care.  
VII.Adoption of Health Information Technology Standards and Incorporation by
Reference
Borinquen Health Center supports CMSâ€™ efforts to ensure ONC-HHS harmonization of health IT 
standards and specifications but urges the agencies to ensure that the HTI-5 final regulations 
conform to CMS-0062-P regulations. Corresponding ONC-HHS standards continue to promote a 
nationwide health IT infrastructure and federal alignment on interoperability and health 
information exchange standards. However, Borinquen Health Center is concerned about how this 
rule conflicts with proposals in the HTI-5 proposed rule. This rule, CMS-0062-P, expands 
interoperability mandates, specifically CRD/DTR/PAS (the HL7 Da Vinci Project Implementation 
Guides (IGs) that automate ePA) v2.2 by October 2027, whereas the HTI-5 proposed rule, 
published early this year, seeks to drastically change the ONC certification program; for instance, 
it proposed removing 34 of 60 certification criteria. While HTI-5 retains the ePA criteria finalized 
in HTI-4 (90 FR 37130, Aug 4, 2025), the broader reduction of 34 certification criteria may affect 
supporting infrastructure â€” such as clinical information reconciliation and security capabilities â€” 
that indirectly enables ePA workflows. Vendors serving safety-net markets may deprioritize non-
required capabilities that CHCs depend on for operational readiness.  
Borinquen Health Center is also concerned about a temporal gap between this proposed 
ruleâ€™s payer compliance deadlines and the availability of certified provider-facing technology. 
CMS-0062-P proposes payer compliance by October 1, 2027, but the EHR certification 
deadlines established under HTI-4 (90 FR 37130) extend to December 2027 and January 
2028 for the ePA certification criteria at 45 CFR 170.315(g)(31)-(g)(33). This creates an 
implementation period of up to three months during which payer APIs may be operational but 
CHC EHR systems may not yet have certified modules available to connect to them. During this 
gap, CHCs and other providers cannot be considered non-compliant for failing to use technology 
that does not yet exist in certified form. 
Borinquen Health Center requests CMS and ONC issue joint implementation guidance ensuring 
any final proposals in HTI-5 do not inadvertently undercut final regulations within this rule, 
CMS-0062-P. We recommend that a formal CMS-ONC harmonization assessment be published 
before the CMS-0062-P final rule.  
Thank you for your consideration of these comments. We are supportive of these provisions that 
will advance ePA, increase timely access to care and essential medication, and promote stronger 
interoperability standard to benefit CHC patients. If you have any questions, please contact 
Diego I. Shmuels, Chief Quality Officer at; dshmuels@borinquenhealth.org
Sincerely, 
Paul Carl Velez, President and CEO 
Borinquen Health Care Center, Inc.

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Borinquen Health Care Center, Inc.; signed by Paul Carl Velez, President and CEO
- **Stakeholder type:** Healthcare Provider
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Federally Qualified Health Center serving medically underserved Miami-Dade County communities since 1972; Level 3 NCQA Patient-Centered Medical Home; accredited by AAAHC and CARF; provides primary care, dental, behavioral health, HIV, pharmacy, podiatry, OB/GYN, and related services.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Borinquen strongly supports CMS's interoperability and drug ePA goals because CHC patients are harmed by prior authorization delays and fragmented payer workflows. It requests realistic timelines, vendor accountability, safety-net funding, cybersecurity support, medical/pharmacy benefit clarity, 340B-aware implementation guidance, proactive PA expiration alerts, automatic approval for missed deadlines, centralized machine-readable endpoint publication, richer API usage metrics, formulary data retention, transition support from X12 to FHIR, CDex guardrails, gold-carding, and CMS-ONC harmonization.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** CMS-0062-P; CMS-0053-F; 45 CFR 170.315(g)(31)-(g)(33); HTI-4, 90 FR 37130; HTI-5 proposed rule; National Standards Group enforcement discretion dated February 28, 2024.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR; HL7 Da Vinci CRD, DTR, PAS v2.2; CDex; X12 278; X12 6020 claims attachments; NCPDP standards generally through pharmacy ePA context; Provider Access, Patient Access, Payer-to-Payer, PA, and Provider Directory APIs; ONC certification criteria.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: API and interoperability implementation for CHCs**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support with modification
- **Rationale:** Standardized APIs can reduce duplicative documentation and improve PA transparency, but CHCs have small IT teams, limited financial flexibility, dependence on vendors, and substantial cybersecurity exposure.
- **Specific request:** Coordinate with ONC, validate readiness before enforcement, set uniform minimum requirements across Medicaid MCOs and QHPs, clarify providers will not be penalized for vendor/clearinghouse/EHR failures outside their control, and provide technical assistance, workforce support, cybersecurity support, and dedicated health IT funding.

**Topic 2: Electronic prior authorization for drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support with modification
- **Rationale:** CHC patients depend on uninterrupted medication access for diabetes, hypertension, behavioral health, HIV, PrEP, antiretroviral therapy, and substance use disorder treatment. However, dual medical/pharmacy workflows and 340B operations make implementation complex.
- **Specific request:** Require payers to expose benefit classification information through Provider Access APIs using the CRD Coverage Information extension; clarify whether PA approval under one benefit pathway applies to the alternate pathway; coordinate with the Office of Pharmacy Affairs on 340B implementation; provide funding and technical assistance.

**Topic 3: PA expiration alerts and broader PA reform**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** ePA can streamline workflows but may not reduce burden if PA volumes remain high or if reauthorization lapses interrupt treatment.
- **Specific request:** Mandate proactive FHIR-based PA expiration notifications and pair ePA mandates with PA reduction tools, including gold-carding for prescription drugs and sunset provisions for high-approval PA categories.

**Topic 4: Communication, denials, and timeframes**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Support with modification
- **Rationale:** Medically underserved patients face worsened outcomes when PA delays interrupt medications or referrals. Specific denial reasons help CHCs correct submissions, appeal, and resubmit without repeated back-and-forth.
- **Specific request:** Maintain 24-hour drug PA timeframes, 7-day standard item/service timeframes, and 72-hour expedited timeframes; require actionable denial reasons; publish PA metrics centrally; add granular burden metrics; and automatically approve PA requests not decided within required timeframes.

**Topic 5: API endpoint reporting**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Support with modification
- **Rationale:** CHC staff now must locate payer endpoint information separately across multiple payer websites, which diverts scarce IT resources and delays integration.
- **Specific request:** Publish endpoint information centrally on CMS's website as machine-readable files; retain the proposed reporting timing, one-week change updates, and annual verification; prioritize ease of access for safety-net and rural providers.

**Topic 6: API usage metrics and PA information retention**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support with modification
- **Rationale:** Program- and plan-level reporting will help identify gaps for Medicaid managed care patients, and richer metrics are needed to evaluate whether APIs actually work in clinical workflows.
- **Specific request:** Require plan/program disaggregation, denial rates, extension timeframes, adjudicated appeals, successful API request rates, rejected requests, authorization failures, malformed queries, calls not received, structured vs. unstructured responses, workflow impact, calls per query, queries per user, and API maintenance costs.

**Topic 7: Drug formulary information in APIs**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Oppose removal / Modify
- **Rationale:** Payer websites are not reliable real-time sources for formulary status, PBMs can change exclusions rapidly, and CHC providers lack staff capacity for manual lookups across payer sites.
- **Specific request:** Reconsider removing drug formulary information from Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs.

**Topic 8: Federal matching funds and safety-net support**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL; STATE-EXTENSION-PROCESS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** CHCs operate on thin margins, incur training and implementation costs, and often have limited cash reserves.
- **Specific request:** Prioritize safety-net providers for available Medicaid/CHIP federal matching funds or related support for training, implementation, staff, clinical training, patient education, and interoperability access.

**Topic 9: HIPAA PA standards and X12-to-FHIR transition**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Support with modification
- **Rationale:** Moving from X12 to FHIR can improve interoperability, but CHCs and clearinghouses may need to support X12 6020 and FHIR/CDex simultaneously, creating a dual-standard burden.
- **Specific request:** Provide transition support for safety-net providers and extend the February 28, 2024 National Standards Group enforcement discretion allowing FHIR PA API use as an X12 278 substitute during the CMS-0062-P transition period.

**Topic 10: CDex, gold-carding, and ONC harmonization**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** CDex can support PA attachments but could enable iterative payer data requests. CMS-0062-P timelines may precede certified provider-facing technology availability under HTI-4/HTI-5.
- **Specific request:** Require payers to specify all documentation in the initial CDex request, limit solicited attachments to two requests before a decision, set response timeframes after attachments, formally recommend broad gold-carding, issue joint CMS-ONC guidance, and publish a harmonization assessment before finalizing CMS-0062-P.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1/S18:** Supports mandatory interoperability standards in concept but requests implementation safeguards, readiness validation, and vendor accountability to avoid indirect provider burden.
- **S2/S3:** Requests synchronized IG and certification timelines and CMS-ONC harmonization so payer deadlines do not precede certified provider-facing technology.
- **S12:** Identifies implementation challenges for drug ePA, including vendor readiness, CHC IT capacity, cybersecurity exposure, EHR/PMS integration, 340B workflows, and payer inconsistency.
- **S14/S19/S22/S25:** Supports pharmacy benefit ePA but emphasizes operational complexity for CHCs, 340B contract pharmacies, PMS/EHR interoperability, and NCPDP/pharmacy ecosystem readiness.
- **S15:** Responds directly by requesting benefit classification data through Provider Access APIs and clarification on drugs covered under both medical and pharmacy benefits.
- **S16:** Supports specific drug PA denial reasons that identify why a request was denied, missing or insufficient information, and actionable resubmission or appeal information.
- **S17:** Requests denial reporting that captures incomplete, inaccurate, or unclear denial notices and supports more structured accountability.
- **S20:** Supports 24-hour decisions for covered outpatient drugs and more consistent expedited timelines.
- **S21:** Supports October 1, 2027 drug PA implementation if paired with vendor readiness, testing, funding, cybersecurity support, and provider protections.
- **S23/S24/S26/S27/S33:** Supports centralized CMS publication of payer API endpoints, machine-readable files, one-week updates after changes, annual verification, and easy access for safety-net providers.
- **S29/S30/S34/S35:** Supports expanded API usage metrics and recommends metrics on API reliability, authorization failures, malformed queries, structured data, workflow impact, query volume, and maintenance costs.
- **S40/S41/S42:** Addresses QHP timelines indirectly by supporting QHP drug PA notice requirements and urging safety-net implementation support.
- **S43:** Supports alignment of PA timeframes across programs and automatic approvals if payers miss deadlines.
- **S44/S46/S47/S48/S49/S50/S51/S53/S54/S55:** Supports moving from X12 to FHIR but requests transition support, enforcement discretion, CDex guardrails, and recognition of small safety-net provider burden.
- **S60/S61/S62/S64/S65:** Requests CMS-ONC harmonization, HTI-5 alignment, readiness assessment, and avoidance of certification gaps that would undermine ePA.
- **S66-S82:** Addresses broader implementation, cybersecurity, telehealth, AI, and patient access implications for CHCs, though not in detail for each RFI.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Clarify providers will not be penalized for vendor, clearinghouse, or EHR failures outside their control.
2. Coordinate CMS timelines with ONC certification and require readiness validation before enforcement.
3. Establish uniform minimum implementation requirements across Medicaid MCOs and QHP issuers.
4. Provide technical assistance, cybersecurity support, IT workforce support, and dedicated health IT funding for CHCs.
5. Require benefit classification information through Provider Access APIs using CRD Coverage Information.
6. Clarify whether a PA approval under one benefit pathway applies to alternate medical/pharmacy payment pathways.
7. Coordinate with OPA on 340B-related implementation and support.
8. Mandate proactive FHIR-based PA expiration alerts.
9. Pair ePA with PA reduction requirements, including gold-carding and sunset provisions for high-approval categories.
10. Require actionable drug PA denial reasons and centralized PA metric publication.
11. Add granular PA reporting for denial rates by service type or medication category, first-pass approval, overturned denials from defective notices, and data quality.
12. Automatically approve PA requests not decided within required timeframes.
13. Publish API endpoints centrally as machine-readable files and require timely updates.
14. Expand API usage metrics to include functionality, usability, reliability, and cost measures.
15. Retain drug formulary information in Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs.
16. Prioritize safety-net providers for federal matching funds or implementation support.
17. Extend NSG enforcement discretion for FHIR PA API use as an X12 278 substitute during transition.
18. Add CDex guardrails: all documentation in the initial request, no drip-feed requests, two-request maximum before decision, and payer response timeframes.
19. Recommend broad payer gold-carding for ePA and extend privileges across all items and services for eligible providers.
20. Publish a CMS-ONC harmonization assessment before finalizing CMS-0062-P.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Safety-net readiness, vendor accountability, cybersecurity exposure, dual medical/pharmacy workflows, 340B operational complexity, inadequate PA reform, unclear denial information, payer deadline noncompliance, endpoint discovery burden, removal of formulary data, dual X12/FHIR standards, CDex drip-feed requests, certification timing gaps, and unfunded implementation costs.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Medication interruptions, chronic disease deterioration, relapse risk for behavioral health/substance use disorder patients, delayed referrals and testing, increased CHC staff burden, inappropriate denials, abandoned treatment, cybersecurity risks, reduced prescribing quality, and inequitable impact on low-income, Medicaid, uninsured, homeless, agricultural worker, Hispanic, and Caribbean patients.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Small IT teams, limited budgets, vendor dependence, cybersecurity staffing gaps, PMS/EHR interoperability limits, terminology and value-set misalignment, multiple payer websites, hard-coded endpoint disruptions, limited certified module availability, and thin CHC operating margins.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** AMA survey finding 94 percent of physicians report PA delays patient care; average PA wait about three days, with nearly one-third waiting longer than one week; MA organizations made nearly 53 million PA determinations in 2024, including more than four million full or partial denials; CHCs serve more than 16 million Medicaid beneficiaries, over 6 million uninsured individuals, 20.5 million low-income individuals, 1.1 million agricultural workers, and over 1.5 million homeless individuals; more than 90 percent of CHC patients have incomes below 200 percent FPL; CHCs serve 3.5 million patients with diabetes, 6.2 million with hypertension, 10 million overweight or obese patients, and 3.2 million with depression or mood disorders; more than 65 percent of CHCs use 340B contract pharmacy arrangements; proactive outreach before PA expiration achieves positive outcomes in 87 percent of cases versus 25 percent without notification; nearly half of CHCs operate with fewer than 90 days cash on hand and one in four report operating margins of negative five percent.
- **Studies or research referenced:** AMA, MGMA, CHC demographic data, pharmacy interoperability stakeholder evidence, studies on pharmacy access to EHR data, and peer-reviewed evidence that ePA can increase PA volumes and time without broader PA reform.
- **Examples provided:** Extended-release buprenorphine billed under pharmacy or medical benefit depending on dispensing/administration; Borinquen medications such as HIV antiretrovirals, PrEP, injectable buprenorphine, insulin, and diabetes medications; Borinquen's 340B pharmacy, home delivery, e-prescribing, refill, and MTM services; CHC staff managing PAs across primary care referrals, behavioral health, specialty medications, and imaging.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** CHCs/FQHCs, Borinquen patients, low-income and underserved communities, Medicaid and uninsured patients, CHC IT staff, providers, pharmacists, contract pharmacies, TPAs, EHR and PMS vendors, payers, CMS, ONC, OPA, clearinghouses, app developers, and safety-net providers.
- **Economic implications:** Implementation requires vendor upgrades, IT integration, cybersecurity investment, training, clinical workflow redesign, patient education, and staff time that CHCs may not be able to absorb without funding or matching support.
- **Technical feasibility:** Feasible if CMS aligns certification timelines, validates readiness, standardizes payer implementation, provides machine-readable endpoints, maintains formulary data, supports 340B/EHR/PMS integration, and supplies CHC technical assistance.
- **Patient care impact:** The comment predicts improved medication adherence, fewer treatment interruptions, better chronic disease management, faster referrals, fewer avoidable hospitalizations, and more equitable access if implementation is supported and payer accountability is strong.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with extensive modifications
- **Tone:** Professional, practical, safety-net focused, and evidence-based
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Borinquen Health Center supports CMS' proposal to establish ePA requirements for prescription drugs." - Context: Overall position on drug ePA.
2. "CMS should clarify that providers will not be penalized for failures attributable to vendors, clearinghouses, or EHR systems outside provider control." - Context: Provider protection request.
3. "Electronic prior authorization alone may not reduce overall administrative burden without concurrent prior authorization reform." - Context: Concern that automation alone can accelerate inefficient workflows.
4. "Borinquen Health Center urges CMS to establish automatic approval for PA requests that are not decided within the required timeframes." - Context: Enforcement recommendation.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - The comment focuses on October 2027 deadlines, certification gaps into December 2027/January 2028, transition support, and readiness validation.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - CHC thin margins, limited cash, implementation costs, training, cybersecurity, and federal funding are major points.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - The comment repeatedly addresses CHC administrative burden, PA staff time, vendor dependence, and workflow redesign.
- [x] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - API expansion and CHC cybersecurity exposure are discussed in detail.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - The comment centers low-income, Medicaid, uninsured, Hispanic, Caribbean, homeless, agricultural worker, and medically underserved patients.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Vendor readiness, PMS/EHR interoperability, API usability, certification gaps, and testing are core concerns.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - FHIR, CRD/DTR/PAS, CDex, X12, and ONC certification maturity and timing are addressed.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Medication delays, chronic disease management, behavioral health continuity, and specialty referrals are central.
- [ ] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - The comment does not challenge CMS/HHS legal authority.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - CMS coordination with ONC, OPA, vendors, payers, and safety-net providers is requested.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - The comment directly requests benefit classification clarity and dual-pathway guidance.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Denial reasons, PA metrics, endpoint publication, formulary information, and API data are major topics.
- [x] **SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT** - The analogous safety-net/small-provider burden is central; small payer impact is not directly addressed.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - 340B, pharmacy, EHR, PMS, clearinghouse, PA, and CHC clinical workflows are extensively discussed.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - EHR vendors, PMS vendors, app developers, clearinghouses, TPAs, and technology partners are central to implementation.
